query: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) is an unmodified α + β dual-phase alloy whose low hardness and poor friction and wear properties limit its use under extreme-service and high-contact-stress conditions. Formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could improve its hardness and wear resistance without sacrificing its existing beneficial properties. State the intervention, proposed mechanism, predicted outcome relative to untreated TC4, applicable operating or test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A two‐stage low‐temperature plasma oxy‐nitriding treatment applied to TC4 (Ti6Al4V) can improve its surface hardness and wear resistance without deteriorating its inherent ductility and corrosion resistance, primarily by enhancing diffusion-controlled kinetics through a disrupted barrier that permits greater nitrogen penetration.
generation.material_initial_state: Unmodified TC4 (Ti6Al4V) alloy with an α+β dual-phase microstructure showing low hardness and poor friction/wear properties.
generation.intervention: A two-stage plasma oxy-nitriding process conducted at a low temperature below the value that induces phase transformation. First, the alloy is exposed to an oxygen-boosted plasma environment for a short duration sufficient to disrupt the formation of a continuous TiN barrier. Next, the environment is switched to a nitrogen-rich plasma (using a suitable NH3-N2 gas mixture) for an additional brief period to promote rapid diffusion of nitrogen and residual oxygen into the substrate.
generation.conditions: The process is carried out at a low temperature kept below the critical threshold for phase transformation; the treatment comprises a brief oxy-nitriding step followed by an additional short nitriding step with a controlled gas mixture and plasma parameters, ensuring that the operating conditions remain within the low-temperature regime specified by the question.
generation.structural_mediator: A compound surface layer comprising non-continuous Ti-N phases intermingled with a porous, interconnected sub-layer that serves as both a hard phase and a buffer to absorb mechanical stresses.
generation.mechanism: The initial oxygen step prevents the formation of a dense, continuous TiN barrier, thereby creating breakpoints that allow more rapid nitrogen diffusion during the subsequent nitriding stage; this enhanced diffusion-controlled kinetics results in a thicker, harder surface layer with a porous substructure that improves wear resistance without severely compromising ductility or corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated TC4 is expected to exhibit a significant increase in surface microhardness and a decreased friction coefficient (improved wear performance) compared to untreated material, while retaining its beneficial mechanical and corrosion properties.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (hardness, friction coefficient, wear rate) of untreated TC4 alloy.
generation.boundary: The benefits are expected when operating the treatment below 700 °C with the specified time durations; deviations to higher temperatures or much longer treatment times may lead to undesirable phase transformations or embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal gas mixture ratios and exact treatment durations may need further fine-tuning; the precise magnitude of improvements (e.g., percentage increases in hardness or wear reduction) is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of TC4 samples: one subjected to the proposed two-stage low-temperature plasma oxy-nitriding treatment and one untreated control group. Test both groups under identical conditions using a ball-on-disc tribometer under high-contact-stress conditions and measure key parameters. Additionally, characterize the surface microstructures and hardness using SEM and microhardness testing.
measurements: Wear volume and wear rate under specified loads
Microstructural characterization (e.g., presence and distribution of Ti-N phases and porous substructures)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated TC4 samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in surface hardness (e.g., an increase of at least 50% relative to untreated samples) as well as a meaningful reduction in wear rate (e.g., a twofold or greater reduction) and lower friction coefficient, then the hypothesis is falsified.

However, they are susceptible to abrasion because of low wear resistance, which is their principal drawback [,]. A novel kind of plasma oxy-nitriding technology at 650 °C was developed in this paper and a thicker permeation coating was obtained on a TC4 alloy compared to conventional plasma nitriding technology. The best process contained two steps oxy-nitriding processes with different ratios of N to O. The introduction of oxygen in the first oxy-nitriding process can prevent the formation of a continuous TiN barrier layer. The breakpoint of the discontinuous TiN layer provided a pathway for the subsequent quick permeation of O and N into the titanium alloy. For the oxy-nitrided sample with 2 h treatment in the first step, an inter-connected porous structure under a compact compound layer was formed, which acts as a buffer layer to absorb the external force. Therefore, the wear performance of the oxy-nitrided sample with a special microstructure showed the lowest COF value during the initial wear state, and almost no debris and cracks were detected after the wear test. On the contrary, for the samples with low hardness and no porous structure, fatigue cracks can be easily formed on the surface and bulk peeling-off can occur during the wear course. The growth of the Ti-N compound layer was enhanced by the use of an NH3-N2 mixture during the plasma nitriding of the Ti6Al4V alloy. After nitriding at 750 °C for 4 h in an NH3-N2 (1:2) atmosphere, a Ti-N compound layer approximately 2 μm thick was formed on the Ti6Al4V alloy. The Ti-N compound layers are typically much harder than the titanium alloy substrate. In comparison to the un-nitrided titanium alloy, samples nitrided in an NH3-N2 mixture exhibited the complete elimination of stick–tear and plowing wear throughout the duration of the test, resulting in undetectable wear loss when in contact with bearing steel. The oxide layer formed on the wear track by the transfer of material from the counterpart steel ball reduced the average friction coefficient from approximately 0.55 to 0.30 under an 8N load. The formation of the Ti-N layer not only enhances the hardness and wear resistance of the titanium alloy but also increases its corrosion resistance.
